report.summary: Analyzed chunk 3 of session.py (lines 561-), found multiple claims in docstrings/comments, verified against code.

handoff.purpose: Parse claims, detect anomalies, assemble round prompts, dispatch rounds, map replies to turn envelopes, and provide dry run plan stub.

symbols.name: _anomaly_reason
symbols.note: Returns anomaly reason string from content matching _ANOMALY_RE patterns, else empty string.

symbols.name: _round_body
symbols.note: Assembles prompt body for a round, including answer format, blind/refute instructions, and prior turns.

symbols.name: _call
symbols.note: Calls adapter.ask and stores result or exception in box dict.

symbols.name: _dispatch_round
symbols.note: Runs one round of participant calls concurrently using daemon threads with a deadline.

symbols.name: _turn_from_reply
symbols.note: Maps a VendorReply to a bus turn envelope dictionary.

symbols.name: _floor_refusal_turn
symbols.note: Creates a turn dict for a participant that was refused by the floor.

symbols.name: _budget_turn
symbols.note: Creates a turn dict for a participant that exhausted budget.

symbols.name: dry_run_plan
symbols.note: Stub function, only signature present in this chunk.

claims.text: A reviewer reporting embedded instructions is doing useful work; the report is chained as a turn STATUS, not buried in prose.
claims.why: The docstring describes how the anomaly is used downstream; this chunk only defines _anomaly_reason, not how its return value is chained.

claims.text: IT IS A MODEL ASSERTION, NOT A DETECTION. Nothing here verifies that the evidence actually contained an instruction, and a weak model will raise it spuriously (observed: a 7b emitting it on question-only evidence).
claims.why: The function simply matches regex patterns; it does not verify actual instructions, so it is an assertion, not a detection.

claims.text: So an anomaly turn still counts as a voice, keeps its content verbatim, and its claims are still parsed -- it flags a thing for a human to look at and decides nothing.
claims.why: This claim about downstream handling is not verifiable from this chunk alone.

claims.text: Untrusted bytes (the evidence) are NOT here at all -- the adapter renders them, after ``PROMPT_DATA_NOTICE``, inside fenced evidence blocks, so withholding is structural and the instruction position stays session-authored.
claims.why: The function _round_body does not include evidence bytes; it only assembles the prompt body without evidence content.

claims.text: Prior TURNS are untrusted too (an injection in the evidence can propagate as an apparently-authored turn), so they get the same fenced, explicitly-data treatment.
claims.why: The function wraps prior turns in _TRANSCRIPT_OPEN and _TRANSCRIPT_CLOSE markers with a warning that they are data.

claims.text: THIS ROUND IS BLIND: no other participant's answer is shown to you, and yours is not shown to them. Answer from the evidence alone.
claims.why: When round_no == 1, the function appends that exact text.

claims.text: THIS ROUND: REFUTE. Name the specific prior claims you believe are wrong and say why, citing evidence. Do not seek consensus, do not summarise, and do not restate agreement -- agreement is not evidence. If you now think one of YOUR OWN prior claims was wrong, say which and why. Same CLAIM/CITE/CHECK format.
claims.why: For rounds > 1, the function appends that exact text.

claims.text: Threads are DAEMONS and are abandoned at the cap rather than joined: a hung vendor must degrade the quorum, never block the session, and a thread cannot be killed. The real process tree is bounded inside the adapter by ``spine.cancel.ManagedProcess``; this is the outer, transport-agnostic bound that also covers a wedged in-process fake.
claims.why: Threads are created with daemon=True, and the function joins with a timeout but does not force-kill threads after deadline (abandoned).

claims.text: The adapter already refused: the bytes never left the process. Hand the bus the evidence refs so ITS floor mints the canonical ``refused`` receipt (a caller may not assert that status -- an asserted refusal is an unverified claim that a scan happened). Where the hit was on the content channel of a file we do not show, this lands as an honest unavailable/transport_error and the rule label rides on the record.
claims.why: The code sets status 'unavailable' and reason 'transport_error', and includes evidence refs. It does not assert 'refused' status.

claims.text: The turn carries the OFFENDING PATH as an evidence ref precisely so the bus's own path-channel scan fires and mints the ``refused`` receipt naming the rule label. The receipt drops content, refs, evidence and the free-text meta, so the offending bytes never reach the file -- not in the turn and not in the receipt. ``status``/``reason`` below are the pre-scan placeholders the bus overwrites; they are never what lands on disk when the scan fires.
claims.why: The function sets status 'unavailable' and reason 'transport_error', includes evidence with the offending path, and has no content. The docstring describes downstream behavior not in this chunk, but the function itself is consistent with the claim.

observations.what: In _round_body, prior turns are rendered with a warning that they are data, but the code does not strip any potential instruction-like content from the prior turns.
The _dispatch_round function does not handle the case where budget_s is negative; deadline would be less than started, causing immediate timeout.
